etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
paragraphs: From Middle English fawne, fowne, foun, from Old French faon, foon, feon, from Vulgar Latin *fētōnem, from Latin fētus (“offspring, young”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁(y)- (“to suckle, nurse”). Displaced native Old English hindċealf (literally “deer calf”). Doublet of fetus.
senses: (intransitive) To give birth to a fawn.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
paragraphs: From Middle English fawnen, from Old English fagnian, alternative form of fæġnian (“to celebrate”), whence Middle English fainen, English fain. Cognate with Old Norse fagna. See also fain.
senses: (literal, of a dog) To show devotion or submissiveness by wagging its tail, nuzzling, licking, etc.
